entry.title: Fotu v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1589
entry.content:
The Federal Court set aside the Assistant Minister’s personal decision under s 501BA(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to override an Administrative Review Tribunal decision and cancel Mr Fotu’s visa. The determinative error was the Minister’s illogical dismissal as “untenable” of the relevance of the applicant’s youth and developing maturity to the risk of reoffending. The decision was quashed on judicial review.

Key holding: Dismissing as “untenable” the evidence-supported relevance of a young offender’s developing maturity to reoffending risk is illogical or irrational and can constitute material jurisdictional error.

I do not consider a logical or rational person would have reached a conclusion that it was untenable to have regard to the applicant's maturity over time in the face of the available evidence.

entry.title: Testart v Testart (No 3) [2026] FCA 1558
entry.content:
This matter concerned Ms Testart’s attempt to vacate a stay and reinstate her Fair Work proceeding after the trustee of her bankrupt estate elected under s 60(2) Bankruptcy Act 1966 (Cth) to discontinue it; the sequestration order was later set aside. The Federal Court treated her application as one to set aside the discontinuance but refused relief because she did not challenge the trustee’s decision within the 60-day period in r 90-80 and gave no sufficient explanation for the delay.

Key holding: A party seeking a late procedural indulgence must satisfactorily explain the delay, and the Court will weigh prejudice and the administration of justice in deciding whether to grant it.

Accordingly, a party who seeks a late procedural indulgence must provide a satisfactory explanation for the delay, and the Court is entitled to consider not only prejudice to the opposing party but also the impact upon the administration of justice and the efficient use of judicial resources: Aon Risk Services Australia Ltd v Australian National University (2009) 239 CLR 175; UBS AG v Tyne (2018) 265 CLR 77.

entry.title: Mills and National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS) [2026] ARTA 2435
entry.content:
Ms Mills, a 54-year-old NDIS participant with a traumatic brain injury, sought additional SIL, active overnight support and SDA. The Tribunal set aside the SOPS decision and substituted supports, including active overnight support for four nights per month, but refused SDA and directed that MAC attendant-care payments be treated as compensation.

Key holding: Where a participant receives attendant-care payments under the Northern Territory MAC scheme, the NDIS should fully fund SIL supports but bring those payments to account as compensation.

The NDIS should fully fund Ms Mills' SIL supports, but take into account the funding to be received by Ms Mills under the Northern Territory MAC scheme as 'compensation.

entry.title: BDCN and Child Support Registrar (Child support second review) [2026] ARTA 2432
entry.content:
This was a second review of child support care percentages for two children. The Father alleged the Mother ceased providing care from January 2024 when the family lost its home, with older daughters and friends said to be providing care. The Tribunal found the Mother continued to arrange and provide care, including delegated care, and affirmed the existing 100% care determination to her.

Key holding: A parent’s percentage of care is not reduced merely because care is temporarily delivered through others or because older children assist, where the parent continues to arrange, financially support and meet the children’s needs.

Taking all of the above matters into account, I am not satisfied that the care of the children actually taking place no longer corresponded with the existing percentage of care determination of 100% to the Mother for each of the 2 children.

entry.title: Australian Securities and Investments Commission v Dawson [2026] FCA 1548
entry.content:
SXHR, a Sri Lankan unauthorised maritime arrival in immigration detention, sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Bridging E visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal had applied Direction No 110 and refused the visa notwithstanding the applicant’s outstanding Ministerial intervention request. The Federal Court dismissed the review.

Key holding: Direction 110 requires comparison of the risk attached to refusal and grant of the visa, but not separate assessment of every possible outcome after grant where only the grant creates a risk of the applicant remaining in the community.

There is no error in that approach; nothing could have been gained by comparing the nature or extent of that risk depending on which of the two identified scenarios following the grant of a visa eventuated. DVRL does not say anything against that.

entry.title: Hoang and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2396
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed the Minister’s refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Hoang’s Class BF Transitional (Permanent) visa under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). Although Mr Hoang had a substantial criminal record for repeat drug and weapons offending and failed the character test, the Tribunal found another reason to revoke under s 501CA(4) and set aside the refusal.

Key holding: A residual risk of reoffending may be acceptable, and another reason to revoke may exist, where serious addiction-related offending is offset by sustained rehabilitation, family support and long residence.

The Applicant has, nonetheless, made significant progress in rehabilitation and has retained the support and trust of his immediate family who are an important element to his future success. I consider that the 'residual' risk of reoffending is acceptable despite the potentially serious consequences for the community, and Mr Hoang's length of residence from a young age must take into account.

entry.title: XTXD and Child Support Registrar (Child support second review) [2026] ARTA 2401
entry.content:
The Administrative Review Tribunal dealt with two second-review applications concerning the percentage of care for a child in a child support assessment. The Father alleged care changed in March 2024 and again in September 2024, while the Mother disputed his account. The Tribunal found an approximate 50/50 care pattern from 7 March 2024 but was not satisfied the later change to full-time care was established.

Key holding: A care percentage may be determined from an overall pattern of recurring care despite an irregular timetable, without identifying every overnight occasion.

An irregular arrangement can constitute a pattern of care where the evidence establishes recurring care, even though the precise timetable of care changes.

entry.title: WNZP and Child Support Registrar (Child support second review) [2026] ARTA 2398
entry.content:
This was a second review in a child support matter concerning the parents’ percentage of care for two children after the Mother notified a change of care on 23 March 2024. The Tribunal recalculated actual care, rejected an argument that the Father’s overseas absences meant he had relinquished care, and declined to record court-ordered care under s 51 because the change predated 29 March 2024. The decision under review was set aside and new care percentages were substituted.

Key holding: Under the law applying before 29 March 2024, an interim care determination under s 51 cannot be made where existing care percentages are revoked under s 54F or s 54H.

I am bound by the Court's interpretation in CMU23 and must apply the legislation in force prior to 29 March 2024, specifically paragraph 53(1)(c), such that an interim determination cannot be made when existing percentages of care are revoked either pursuant to section 54F or section 54H of the Act.

entry.title: Lye v Comcare [2026] FCA 1517
entry.content:
This was a Federal Court appeal from an Administrative Review Tribunal decision concerning weekly compensation under the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Act 1988 (Cth). The Tribunal had equated Mr Lye’s capacity to work full-time usual hours in administrative duties with an ability to earn his normal weekly earnings, reducing compensation to zero. The Court found legal error and, by consent, set aside the decision and remitted the matter for redetermination.

Key holding: Under s 19(2) of the SRC Act, the Tribunal must separately assess the amount per week the employee is able to earn in suitable employment and use that to determine the reduction to NWE; merely equating capacity for normal hours with NWE is legal error.

In its reasons at [40], the Tribunal failed to address the amount per week (if any) that the applicant was able to earn in suitable employment during the relevant periods (i.e., the fourth question). As a result of the above failure, the Tribunal failed properly to address the amount (if any) by which the applicant's NWE should be reduced in order to determine the amount of compensation that he is entitled to receive (i.e., the sixth question).

entry.title: Mohamedali v Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1531
entry.content:
The Federal Court allowed a consent judicial review application concerning a decision by the Assistant Minister under s 501BA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to cancel the applicant’s visa. The Assistant Minister conceded jurisdictional error because he failed to consider an updated psychologist’s report that was constructively before him and relevant to the applicant’s risk of reoffending. The Court made orders quashing the cancellation decision.

Key holding: A s 501BA decision is affected by jurisdictional error if the Minister fails to properly consider material constructively before him that is relevant to the risk the applicant poses to the Australian community and the national interest.

Accordingly, the Assistant Minister accepts that his decision was affected by jurisdictional error as a result of his failure to properly consider the risk the applicant posed to the Australian community.

entry.title: Smith v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1520
entry.content:
Mr Smith, a New Zealand citizen, had his Class TY Subclass 444 visa cancelled under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) after criminal convictions and imprisonment. A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation, and the Administrative Review Tribunal affirmed that refusal. On judicial review, the Federal Court found the Tribunal misconstrued Direction 110’s definition of “family violence” and set aside its decision.

Key holding: Conduct falling within an example of family violence in Direction 110 cl 4 is not automatically family violence; it must also have the effect of coercing or controlling a family member or causing that person to be fearful.

For example, behaviour which involves "intentionally damaging or destroying property" will not necessarily constitute family violence. It will only do so if that behaviour had the effect of coercing or controlling a member of the perpetrator's family, or causing the family member or members to be fearful.

entry.title: Jaworski v Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand (No 2) [2026] NSWCA 213
entry.content:
Mr Jaworski sought to set aside or vary the Court of Appeal’s earlier leave judgment under UCPR r 36.16, and CA ANZ sought gross sum costs. The Court dismissed the reopening application and fixed costs at $30,000 for the leave/recusal application and $6,000 for CA ANZ’s notice of motion. The dispute concerned alleged errors, bias/prejudgment and costs in ongoing litigation involving CA ANZ.

Key holding: Under UCPR r 36.16, reopening requires some error in the court's reasoning due to misapprehension of fact or law that is not solely attributable to the applicant's neglect or default.

What is required to be established on an application under r 36.16 is some error in the court's reasoning because of a misapprehension of the facts or misapprehension of the relevant law; and that this misapprehension cannot be attributed solely to the neglect or default of the party seeking the rehearing.

entry.title: Huseni and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Citizenship) [2026] ARTA 2420
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a refusal of Australian citizenship by conferral on good character grounds under s 21(2)(h) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth). The Minister alleged the applicant failed to declare alternative names and provided undeclared migration assistance through his company, Immi Solution. The Tribunal found no dishonest intent and no proven personal provision of immigration assistance, and was satisfied the applicant was of good character.

Key holding: For s 21(2)(h), good character requires a holistic assessment of enduring moral qualities and is not negated by every acknowledged mistake or oversight, particularly where there is no fraud or dishonesty.

His actions, when considered on an individual or cumulative basis, are regrettable but do not reach the threshold of being demonstrative of someone who is presently not of good character.

entry.title: South Australian Commission for Catholic Schools Inc and Secretary, Department of Education (Guidance and Appeals Panel) [2026] ARTA 2304
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed 2024 Commonwealth recurrent funding determinations for 84 non-government Catholic schools in South Australia. It unanimously held that mid-year reception students who began in term 3 2024 were “primary students” because reception was the “foundation” year of schooling immediately before year 1. A majority then held those students did not have a pattern of regular attendance at school or school generally during 2024, so they failed reg 9B(1)(c) and were ineligible unless the Minister included them under reg 9B(3).

Key holding: Reception undertaken by mid-year reception students is the “foundation” year of schooling immediately before year 1, so those students are primary students in that calendar year.

Giving the phrases to which I have already referred their natural meaning, the logical conclusion is that the 2024 mid-year reception students were in the year of schooling in a course of primary education that was immediately before year 1. It follows that, in 2024, those students were in the foundation year of schooling, were receiving primary education and were therefore primary students at their school.

entry.title: Tran and Australian Skills Quality Authority [2026] ARTA 2300
entry.content:
Mr Tran sought review of ASQA’s decision to cancel his Certificate III in Carpentry, obtained via RPL from Kingsway, a deregistered RTO. Although the Tribunal found the s 56(1)(a) ground was established because Kingsway did not provide or arrange the necessary assessment, it exercised the discretion not to cancel in exceptional circumstances. The cancellation decision was set aside and the qualification is to be treated as a valid VET RPL qualification.

Key holding: Even when the s 56(1)(a) ground is established, the Tribunal may exercise the s 56(1) discretion not to cancel a VET qualification in exceptional circumstances, including clear lack of applicant fault, misleading RTO conduct, extensive genuine industry experience, and a public interest that does not require cancellation.

The Tribunal is satisfied that the discretion under subsection 56(1) of the NVR Act not to cancel the Qualification can be safely and appropriately exercised in the exceptional circumstances of this case. That discretion may be exercised consistent with the public interest, given that Mr Tran possesses the requisite training, skills and work experience to have been awarded the Qualification on an RPL basis.

entry.title: Niven and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2274
entry.content:
This was a merits review of a delegate’s decision not to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Niven’s Class TY Subclass 444 Special Category (Temporary) visa under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal found the applicant did not pass the character test but accepted there was another reason to revoke the cancellation, set aside the delegate’s decision, and substituted a decision revoking the cancellation.

Key holding: Under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), where an applicant fails the character test, the Tribunal may revoke mandatory cancellation if satisfied there is another reason, applying Direction no. 110.

Section 501CA(4) states that the Minister may revoke the original decision if: (a) the person makes representations in accordance with the invitation; and (b) the Minister is satisfied: (i) that the person passes the character test (as defined by s 501); or (ii) that there is another reason why the original decision should be revoked.

entry.title: Kintanar (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2384
entry.content:
In Kintanar (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2384, the Tribunal reviewed a refusal of a Partner (Temporary) (Class UK)/Subclass 820 visa because the applicant’s non-migrating child, Leonel, failed PIC 4007 due to severe cognitive impairment/autism and an estimated care cost of $1,577,840. The Tribunal found the MOC opinion valid but waived the health criterion under PIC 4007(2)(b), weighing the child’s non-migrating status, the applicant’s and sponsor’s regional NSW contributions, and their capacity to mitigate future costs.

Key holding: Under PIC 4007(2)(b), the Tribunal may waive the health criterion where the benefits and contributions of the applicant and sponsor, the detriment of refusal, and the applicant’s capacity to mitigate future costs outweigh a cost that cannot be realised from the grant of the visa alone.

The Tribunal concludes that the benefits that the visa applicant and her partner bring to the Australian community, the detriment to the visa sponsor and his family if the visa was refused and the applicant and sponsor's capacity to mitigate the potential costs to the Australia community should Leonel apply for a visa in the future to join his mother, outweigh a cost to the Australian community which cannot be realised from the grant of this visa alone.

entry.title: Upson and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2275
entry.content:

A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation, but the Administrative Review Tribunal set that decision aside and substituted revocation after finding “another reason” under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii).

Key holding: Under Direction no. 110, whether a non-citizen poses an “unacceptable risk” is a distinct evaluative conclusion reached by balancing the likelihood and potential harm of future offending, not merely the likelihood of re-offending.

The concept of 'risk', and whether it is 'unacceptable', under cl 8.1.2(1) of the Direction is not the same thing as the 'likelihood of the non-citizen engaging in further criminal or other serious conduct'.[25]

entry.title: Austro Enterprises Pty Limited (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2379
entry.content:
Austro Enterprises Pty Limited sought review of a delegate’s refusal to approve a nomination for Mr Erich Martinez as Office Manager under the Core Skills stream of the Subclass 482 visa. The delegate found the position was not genuine under reg 2.72(10) because existing roles allegedly covered the duties. The Tribunal accepted the position was genuine and remitted the nomination for reconsideration.

Key holding: Whether a position is genuine under reg 2.72(10)(a) requires a qualitative, reality-tested comparison between the actual position and the nominated occupation, not merely paper duties.

Regulation 2.72(10)(a) requires that the position associated with the nominated occupation is genuine. A similar requirement was considered in Cargo First Pty Ltd v MIBP [2016] FCA 30, where the Court (at [34]) upheld the Tribunal's approach of qualitatively assessing the position and comparing this with the occupation nominated in order to determine whether it was genuine.

entry.title: Sharma v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 269 (17 March 2026)
entry.content:
Mr Sharma sought a Regional Sponsored Migration Scheme (subclass 187) visa based on a nomination by Shivram Australia Pty Ltd. The nomination was refused/withdrawn, so the Tribunal affirmed the visa refusal because cl 187.233(3) required an approved nomination, and the Federal Circuit and Family Court dismissed judicial review. On appeal to the Federal Court, Mr Sharma alleged the Tribunal and primary judge failed to engage with his claims that he was defrauded by the nominator and denied natural justice.

Key holding: Third-party fraud does not amount to jurisdictional error unless it stultifies or otherwise affects the decision-maker’s exercise of statutory power; the mandatory approved-nomination criterion remains determinative.

There was no such approved nomination application at the time that the Minister and thereafter the Tribunal considered Mr Sharma's application. Accordingly, whatever the alleged fraud may have been that occurred before the nomination application was refused and the circumstances in which the nominator's review application was withdrawn, that alleged fraud did not affect the Tribunal's, and thereafter the FCFCOA's, power to carry out their respective statutory tasks.

entry.title: San Bao Pty Ltd v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] HCA 6 (11 March 2026)
entry.content:
San Bao Pty Ltd sought constitutional writs of certiorari and mandamus in the High Court after a delegate refused its nomination of Ms Haiming Du for a Subclass 482 (Skills in Demand) visa, the Company having missed the 28-day ART review period. The Company alleged the delegate constructively failed to exercise jurisdiction or acted unreasonably by refusing the nomination on the supposed basis that no organisational chart or staffing-structure evidence had been provided.

Key holding: A decision-maker’s reasons must be read as a whole and in context; a reference to an absent organisational chart does not establish that the decision-maker mistakenly believed no chart was provided where the actual concern was insufficient evidence of how the nominated role fitted the staffing structure.

When the references by the delegate in their reasons to an "organisation[al] chart" are properly understood in their context, it can be seen that the delegate was concerned with the absence of sufficient evidence, including from an organisational chart, that explained the need for an additional cook by detailing the relationship that the additional cook would have within the existing structure.
